title: AI for the Fortune 2000: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native SDLC — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
subtitle: Paying for outcomes, building with agents, and the last mile of enterprise AI adoption
intro: Last year , Alex Lieberman and his cofounder joined us to explain Tenex’s unusual bet: pay AI engineers for the work they deliver, rather than the hours they spend at a keyboard. If AI makes an engineer faster, an hourly rate can make the engineer less money for the same job. Tenex wanted the incentives to run the other way.

At AIE New York, Alex came back with CJ Hess to talk about what happens when you scale that idea into an engineering organization. We also put one of our own experiments on the table: Kill My SaaS , where we asked builders to replace a conference speaker-management tool we were quoted $43,000 a year to use.
Both stories raise the same question: when building gets cheaper, how do you decide what good work is worth?

Tenex still uses story points as an important part of engineering compensation. Alex says the feared failure modes—people inflating estimates or shipping bad code to rack up points—haven’t been the biggest problem. Tenex’s AI strategists are responsible for customer retention and growth, giving them an incentive to push back on work that doesn’t serve the client.

The harder question is how to reward work that doesn’t fit neatly into a ticket: understanding a customer’s problem, designing an architecture, or deciding what should be built in the first place. CJ describes spending less time directly coding as models get better, and more time getting the customer’s context into a form the model can use. A compensation system designed around shipped tasks has to make room for that work too.

Alex says Tenex has grown to 75 people, with customers split between Fortune 2000 companies and mid-market businesses. The firm started as an AI-powered development shop; increasingly, customers are asking for help with AI transformation across the company. Jump to the compensation discussion →

CJ walks through Tenex’s MetaHarness : a shared set of skills, project documents and a CLI around the work. Plans and decisions are checked into Git alongside the code. When an agent comes back to a task, it can read not just what was built, but why the team chose to build it that way.
Tenex’s own AI-native SDLC article shows the idea as a project record that humans and agents work against, with views into Linear, GitHub and client updates:
Source: Tenex, Building an AI-Native SDLC .

The useful distinction is between making agents write code faster and making the surrounding work legible: the plan, acceptance criteria, decisions and evidence. Tenex’s article also notes the cost: that much structure can be overkill for a small team on one project. CJ explains the workflow →

Our Kill My SaaS episode covered 72 submissions to replace our speaker-management software. The team that won with our human judges came 19th on our AI judge’s leaderboard. It was a useful reminder that checking whether software satisfies a list of scenarios and judging whether people want to use it are different jobs.

I brought the project to Alex as a real example of a company choosing to build its own software. His pushback: the further upmarket you go, the more expensive and risky it becomes to rip out an established system. And even for a smaller tool, someone has to maintain it. Is the saving big enough to justify that ongoing attention?

My answer is that the upside isn’t just the bill. Our team has lived with a mediocre product for a long time. If we own the workflow, we can make it better for speakers and operators and iterate in minutes instead of waiting months for a vendor. That potential has to be weighed against the maintenance Alex describes. Watch the exchange →

Alex is generally bearish on vertical-specific AI products: if every enterprise expects a one-of-one solution, how do you deliver that at software margins? And as frontier models improve, how much of the underlying task gets absorbed by general-purpose tools?

I pushed back with examples like Harvey and OpenEvidence. Domain-specific data, specialized interfaces, integrations and user habits can matter even when the underlying model is available to everyone. Bloomberg is a useful comparison: a trader can get market data elsewhere, but the terminal brings data, workflows, communication and existing habits together.

CJ draws a distinction between a vertical product whose main feature is an agent performing a task, and a tool that improves the actual workflow around that task. That leaves a more interesting question than whether “vertical AI” wins or loses: which products become a durable place people do their work, and which become a feature of the agent they already use? Watch the debate →

Tenex — Alex and CJ’s applied AI company, working with enterprises on AI adoption and engineering. Alex Lieberman on Tenex — Alex’s introduction to the company and its approach. Building an AI-native SDLC — Tenex’s explanation of its agent-assisted development process and MetaHarness. Our earlier conversation with Alex and Arman — Tenex’s original case for paying AI engineers for output. Kill My SaaS — What we learned replacing a $43K-a-year speaker-management tool with AI agents.

summary.one_liner: Tenex 探討 AI 原生軟體開發流程、以產出計酬的工程組織設計，以及企業自建軟體與垂直 AI 的取捨。

topics.title: 產出導向的工程計酬模式
topics.body: Tenex 採取依工程交付成果（story points）而非鍵盤工時給薪，避免 AI 提升效率反而讓工程師減薪的逆向激勵。Alex 指出工程師灌水估點或交付爛 code 並非最大問題，因為 AI 策略師需對客戶留存負責。真正的難題是如何獎勵難以票務化（ticket）的架構設計與客戶問題釐清等前期工作。

topics.title: MetaHarness 與上下文顯性化
topics.body: CJ 介紹 Tenex 的 MetaHarness 框架，透過 Git 將計畫、決策紀錄與程式碼一同版本控管。當 Agent 重新接手任務時，不僅能讀取寫了什麼程式碼，更能理解當初決策的原因。這項 AI-native SDLC 的核心價值，在於將圍繞開發的驗收標準與決策脈絡轉化為人類與 Agent 都能看懂的結構化記錄。

topics.title: 自建軟體與維護成本的權衡
topics.body: 主持人分享以 AI 競賽「Kill My SaaS」嘗試取代年費 43,000 美元的會議講者管理工具。Alex 對此提出質疑，認為客群越走向大企業，汰換既有系統的成本與風險就越高，且自建工具仍需長期維護成本。主持人則主張掌握工作流程能帶來自主權，能在數分鐘內迭代改善平庸體驗，而非枯等外部供應商。

topics.title: AI 評測與人類體驗的落差
topics.body: 在 Kill My SaaS 的 72 個參賽作品中，獲得人類評審冠軍的團隊在 AI 評審排行榜上僅名列第 19 名。這項結果凸顯出自動化評估軟體是否符合一系列驗收場景（scenarios），與真實使用者是否願意使用該軟體，本質上是完全不同的兩件事。

topics.title: 垂直領域 AI 的產品護城河
topics.body: Alex 普遍看淡垂直領域 AI 產品，質疑若每家企業都需要高度客製化方案，軟體利潤率將難以維持，且底層任務容易被通用基礎模型吸收。CJ 則指出關鍵在於區分「僅讓 Agent 代替執行任務」與「真正改善整體工作流」的工具。能否成為使用者長期停留的工作介面，決定了它是獨立產品還是被吸收為通用 Agent 的一項功能。

insights.title: 將決策脈絡版本化控管
insights.body: 在設計 Agent 協作工作流時，應將架構計畫、決策理由與驗收標準如程式碼般納入版本控制（Git），讓 Agent 能讀取完整上下文而不僅是靜態程式碼。

insights.title: 工程師價值轉移至上下文整理
insights.body: 隨著模型生成程式碼能力提升，AI 工程師的核心工作正轉向如何將客戶模糊的業務需求，轉化為模型能精準理解與執行的結構化 context。

insights.title: 垂直工具應鎖定工作流程整合
insights.body: 打造垂直領域 AI 或 Agent 系統時，單純封裝任務執行容易被基礎模型取代；應結合特定領域數據、既有工作習慣與整合介面，成為用戶不可或缺的工作介面。

insights.title: 自動化評估無法完全取代使用者體驗
insights.body: 建構 RAG 或 Agent 評測流程時，不能僅依賴 scenario-based 的自動評分，必須建立與實際終端使用者滿意度對齊的驗證機制。

guests.name: Alex Lieberman
guests.intro: Tenex 共同創辦人，帶領團隊以新型工程組織架構協助 Fortune 2000 與中型企業落地 AI 轉型。

guests.name: CJ Hess
guests.intro: 任職於 Tenex，專注於推動 MetaHarness 架構與 AI-native SDLC 的工程實踐。

summary.one_liner: Tenex explores AI-native software development lifecycles, output-based engineering organizational design, and the trade-offs between custom in-house software and vertical AI.

topics.title: Output-Oriented Engineering Compensation Model
topics.body: Tenex compensates based on engineering deliverables (story points) rather than keyboard hours, avoiding the perverse incentive where AI efficiency gains lead to pay cuts for engineers. Alex notes that engineers inflating point estimates or shipping bad code isn't the biggest issue, as AI strategists are held accountable for customer retention. The real challenge is how to reward upfront work that is hard to ticket, such as architectural design and scoping customer problem spaces.

topics.title: MetaHarness and Context Externalization
topics.body: CJ introduces Tenex's MetaHarness framework, which version-controls plans, decision records, and code together via Git. When an agent resumes a task, it doesn't just read the written code—it also understands the rationale behind past decisions. The core value of this AI-native SDLC lies in turning acceptance criteria and decision context into structured records interpretable by both humans and agents.

topics.title: Trade-offs Between In-House Software and Maintenance Costs
topics.body: The host shares an attempt from the AI hackathon 'Kill My SaaS' to replace a $43,000/year conference speaker management tool. Alex pushes back, arguing that as the customer base shifts toward enterprise, the cost and risk of ripping and replacing existing systems rise sharply, and internal tools still carry long-term maintenance overhead. The host counters that owning the workflow grants autonomy, enabling teams to iterate and fix mediocre experiences in minutes rather than waiting endlessly on third-party vendors.

topics.title: The Disconnect Between AI Evals and Human Experience
topics.body: Among the 72 submissions in Kill My SaaS, the team crowned champion by human judges ranked only 19th on the AI judge leaderboard. This outcome highlights that automatically evaluating whether software satisfies a set of acceptance scenarios is fundamentally different from whether real users actually want to use the product.

topics.title: Product Moats for Vertical AI
topics.body: Alex is generally bearish on vertical AI products, questioning whether software margins can be sustained if every enterprise requires highly customized solutions, and noting that underlying tasks are easily commoditized by general foundation models. CJ counters that the key is distinguishing between tools that 'merely have an agent perform a task' versus those that 'fundamentally improve the entire workflow.' Whether a tool becomes the primary interface where users spend their working hours dictates whether it survives as a standalone product or gets absorbed as a feature of general-purpose agents.

insights.title: Version-Control Decision Context
insights.body: When designing agent collaboration workflows, treat architectural plans, decision rationales, and acceptance criteria like code by keeping them under version control (Git), allowing agents to access full context rather than just static code.

insights.title: Engineer Value Shifts Toward Context Curation
insights.body: As model code-generation capabilities advance, the core job of an AI engineer is shifting toward translating ambiguous business requirements into structured context that models can accurately parse and execute.

insights.title: Vertical Tools Must Target Workflow Integration
insights.body: When building vertical AI or agent systems, merely wrapping task execution leaves you vulnerable to being commoditized by foundation models. Instead, combine domain-specific data, established user habits, and deeply integrated interfaces to become an indispensable operational surface for users.

insights.title: Automated Evaluations Cannot Fully Replace User Experience
insights.body: When building RAG or agent evaluation pipelines, do not rely solely on scenario-based automated scoring; establish validation mechanisms aligned with actual end-user satisfaction.

guests.name: Alex Lieberman
guests.intro: Co-founder of Tenex, leading the team in helping Fortune 2000 and mid-market enterprises implement AI transformations through new engineering organizational structures.

guests.name: CJ Hess
guests.intro: Works at Tenex, focusing on driving the engineering practices of the MetaHarness architecture and the AI-native SDLC.
